newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS - POLAND IMMUNE TO CZECH-STYLE SLUMP - FINMIN.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - POLAND IMMUNE TO CZECH-STYLE SLUMP - FINMIN.

text.p: Poland's financial system will not be harmed by the Czech crown slump, which prompted speculators to sell treasuries in the region, Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Wedenesday.

The Czech-style failure -- a soaring balance of payments deficit coupled with economic growth slump, which prompted speculators' onslaught on the crown and forced its devaluation -- will not be repeated in Poland, Belka told a news conference.
Increasingly optimistic foreign trade data and good macroeconomic fundamentals make Poland immune to economic troubles experienced by its southern neighbour, he said.

Belka estimated that a total of $1.2 billion short-term speculative capital was in Poland and said that even if all short-term investors pulled out from zloty instruments the national currency would stay stable. Total foreign currency reserves in the banking system amounted to $21 billion.

"Events of recent days showed that Poland's financial system is very immune to these shocks. I estimate that even if all short-term capital left Poland, it would have only a minor effect on the zloty exchange rate," he said.

The crown crisis triggerred profit-taking on Polish securities but the zloty fell as a result only two percent and the central bank's small-scale intervention late last week easily stopped the decline, he said.

Belka said he felf confident about Poland's economic prospects because strong industrial output growth was accompanied by falling inflation seen at below 15 percent year-on-year inflation in May and falling to 13 percent or less at the end of year.
Growth was seen at 5.5 percent or more this year and about five percent in 1998.
The mounting trade deficit remained the government's main concern, Belka said.
But this month's slow down in credit growth resulting from the central bank's tightening of monetary policy should slow imports and allow to keep trade gap under control, he said.
In 1996 imports rose by more than 30 percent while exports grew about nine percent.

Poland, like the Czech Republic, last year and early in 1997 saw a consumer boom, fuelled by rapid credit expansion, which kept growth at strong six percent last year against seven percent in 1995 despite a much slower pace of exports.
Polish current account gap is expected to rise to 3-3.5 percent of GDP this year from one percent in 1996.

Deputy economy minister Janusz Kaczurba, also present, said he expected Poland to post trade deficits in the next several years and the government would soon send to parliament a set of pro-export measures.

He confirmed the package included an increase in guarantees extended by the finance ministry's Exports Credit Insurance Corporation (KUKE) and incentives for banks to credit purchases of components needed for exports production.
The measures would also provide for setting up an export-import bank and one of state-owned banks could act as such an institution, Kaczurba said without elaborating.
Reputable trading companies would be offered quicker and simplified customs clearance procedures and the government will create an agency to promote Polish goods abroad.
